lessons.title: Ordinal Numbers — Position Words from 1st to 20th
lessons.notes_html:
What are ordinal numbers?

Rule: Ordinal numbers tell the position of things in a row. They answer the question: at what place does this thing stand?

The ordinal numbers from first to twentieth are:

  • 1st = first
  • 2nd = second
  • 3rd = third
  • 4th = fourth
  • 5th = fifth
  • 6th = sixth
  • 7th = seventh
  • 8th = eighth
  • 9th = ninth
  • 10th = tenth
  • 11th = eleventh
  • 12th = twelfth
  • 13th = thirteenth
  • 14th = fourteenth
  • 15th = fifteenth
  • 16th = sixteenth
  • 17th = seventeenth
  • 18th = eighteenth
  • 19th = nineteenth
  • 20th = twentieth

In the book, honey bees flying to their hive show these positions: the bee nearest the hive is 1st (first), the next is 2nd (second), and so on up to the 20th (twentieth) bee.

Remember

Counting numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) tell how many. Ordinal numbers (1st, 2nd, 3rd, ...) tell the position.

mcqs.q: What do ordinal numbers tell us?
options: The position of things in a row
mcqs.why: Ordinal numbers answer the question: at what place does this thing stand? They tell the position, not how many.

mcqs.q: The ordinal number 1st is written in words as
mcqs.why: 1st = first. The list starts: 1st = first, 2nd = second, 3rd = third.

mcqs.q: The ordinal number 5th is written in words as
mcqs.why: Count the positions: 1st first, 2nd second, 3rd third, 4th fourth, 5th fifth.

mcqs.q: The ordinal number 9th is written in words as
mcqs.why: 8th = eighth, 9th = ninth, 10th = tenth, so the 9th position is called ninth.

mcqs.q: The ordinal number 12th is written in words as
mcqs.why: 11th = eleventh, 12th = twelfth, 13th = thirteenth, so 12th is twelfth.

mcqs.q: The ordinal number 20th is written in words as
mcqs.why: The list ends at 20th = twentieth; 19th = nineteenth comes just before it.

mcqs.q: In the book, the honey bee nearest the hive is at which position?
mcqs.why: The bee nearest the hive is 1st (first); the next is 2nd, and so on up to the 20th bee.

mcqs.q: Which numbers tell us how many things there are?
mcqs.why: Counting numbers (1, 2, 3, ...) tell how many. Ordinal numbers tell the position instead.

mcqs.q: The ordinal number 3rd is written in words as
mcqs.why: 1st = first, 2nd = second, 3rd = third, 4th = fourth.

mcqs.q: The ordinal number 15th is written in words as
mcqs.why: 14th = fourteenth, 15th = fifteenth, 16th = sixteenth, so 15th is fifteenth.

lessons.title: Exercise 1 — Alphabet Positions
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Every letter of the alphabet has a fixed position. A is the 1st letter, B is the 2nd, and so on. To find a letter's position, count the letters from A up to that letter.

Worked examples — position of each letter

  • A = 1st
  • B = 2nd
  • C = 3rd
  • D = 4th
  • E = 5th
  • F = 6th
  • G = 7th
  • H = 8th
  • I = 9th
  • J = 10th
  • K = 11th
  • L = 12th
  • M = 13th
  • N = 14th
  • O = 15th
  • P = 16th
  • Q = 17th
  • R = 18th
  • S = 19th
  • T = 20th

How to check one: for the letter T — count A(1), B(2), C(3), D(4), E(5), F(6), G(7), H(8), I(9), J(10), K(11), L(12), M(13), N(14), O(15), P(16), Q(17), R(18), S(19), T(20). So T stands at the 20th position.

mcqs.q: What is the position of the letter A in the alphabet?
mcqs.why: A is the first letter, so A = 1st. Every letter has a fixed position counted from A.

mcqs.q: What is the position of the letter E?
mcqs.why: Count from A: A(1), B(2), C(3), D(4), E(5). So E stands at the 5th position.

mcqs.q: What is the position of the letter J?
What is the position of the letter M?
mcqs.why: Counting from A: K is 11th, L is 12th, M is 13th and N is 14th.

mcqs.q: What is the position of the letter T?
mcqs.why: Count all the letters from A to T: S is 19th and T is the 20th letter.

mcqs.q: Which letter stands at the 7th position?
mcqs.why: A(1), B(2), C(3), D(4), E(5), F(6), G(7). The 7th letter is G.

mcqs.q: Which letter stands at the 16th position?
mcqs.why: Counting from A: N is 14th, O is 15th, P is 16th and Q is 17th.

mcqs.q: What is the position of the letter Q?
mcqs.why: P is the 16th letter and the next letter Q is the 17th letter.

mcqs.q: How do we find the position of a letter?
options: Count the letters from Z backwards

mcqs.why: To find a letter's position, count the letters from A up to that letter, like T counted up to 20.

mcqs.q: What is the position of the letter H?
mcqs.why: Count: F(6), G(7), H(8), I(9). So H stands at the 8th position.

lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Every number can be written in two ways: in numerals (11, 26, 43) and in words (eleven, twenty-six, forty-three). For two-digit numbers, first write the tens word, then the ones word: 28 = twenty + eight = Twenty-eight.

Worked examples — the missing numerals and words on the book's pages

Page 5: the missing numerals are 31, 38, 40, 47, 50, 59. The missing words are: 43 = Forty-three; 44 = Forty-four; 48 = Forty-eight; 49 = Forty-nine; 58 = Fifty-eight.

Page 6: the missing numerals are 63, 66, 72, 73, 79, 85, 90. The missing words are: 62 = Sixty-two; 74 = Seventy-four; 77 = Seventy-seven; 80 = Eighty.

Page 7: the missing numerals are 95, 98. The missing words are: 99 = Ninety-nine; 100 = One Hundred.

Key facts

  • 9 is the greatest 1-digit number.

lessons.title: Three-Digit Numbers — Hundreds
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

10 ones make 1 ten.
10 tens make 100 ones, that is, 1 hundred.
So 100 is the smallest 3-digit number.

Hundreds run from 100 to 900: 100, 200, 300, 400, 500, 600, 700, 800, 900. A 3-digit number is read as: hundreds word, then the tens and ones together.

Worked examples — reading numbers shown in blocks

  • 126 = one hundred twenty-six (1 hundred, 2 tens, 6 ones)
  • 342 = three hundred forty-two (3 hundreds, 4 tens, 2 ones)
  • 999 = nine hundred ninety-nine — this is the greatest 3-digit number

mcqs.why: 10 tens = 10 x 10 = 100 ones. So 10 tens make 1 hundred.

lessons.title: Place Value — Hundreds, Tens and Ones
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

The place value of a digit depends on its place in the number. In a 3-digit number: the first digit from the right is in the ones place, the next is in the tens place, and the next is in the hundreds place. A number can be split into the values of its places.

Worked examples

  • 26 = 20 + 6 (2 tens and 6 ones)
  • 245 = 200 + 40 + 5 (2 hundreds, 4 tens, 5 ones)
  • 308 = 3 hundreds, 0 tens, 8 ones
  • 400 = 4 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones
  • 333 = 300 + 30 + 3 (Try Yourself)

Value of a coloured digit

Look at the place where the coloured digit stands, then write its value.

  • In 472, the digit 4 stands in the hundreds place, so its value is 400.
  • In 238, the digit 3 stands in the tens place, so its value is 30.

lessons.title: Comparison and Ordering of Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
The rules

  • A number with more digits is the greater number. A 3-digit number is always greater than a 2-digit number.
  • When both numbers have the same number of digits, compare the hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones.
  • Ascending order means writing numbers from smallest to greatest. Descending order means writing numbers from greatest to smallest.

Worked examples

435 and 85: 435 has 3 digits and 85 has 2 digits, so 435 > 85.

518 and 376: hundreds are 5 and 3; 5 > 3, so 518 > 376. (The book prints 375 once — that is a misprint for 376.)

368 and 321: hundreds are equal (3 = 3); tens are 6 and 2; 6 > 2, so 368 > 321.

469 and 463: hundreds equal, tens equal; ones are 9 and 3; 9 > 3, so 469 > 463.

Ordering examples

Numbers 235, 516, 147 → Ascending: 147, 235, 516. Descending: 516, 235, 147.

Numbers 162, 203, 168 → Ascending: 162, 168, 203. Descending: 203, 168, 162.

mcqs.why: A number with more digits is the greater number. 435 has 3 digits and 85 has 2 digits, so 435 > 85.

mcqs.q: Which number is greater, 518 or 376?
mcqs.why: Compare the hundreds first: 5 > 3, so 518 > 376.

options: the tens digit 6 is greater than the tens digit 2
mcqs.why: The hundreds are equal (3 = 3), so compare the tens: 6 > 2, so 368 > 321.

mcqs.why: Ascending order means writing numbers from smallest to greatest.

mcqs.why: Smallest to greatest: 147 < 235 < 516, so ascending order is 147, 235, 516.

mcqs.why: A number with more digits is greater, so any 3-digit number (100 to 999) is greater than any 2-digit number.

mcqs.why: With equal digits, compare the hundreds first, then the tens, then the ones.

mcqs.q: The numbers 235, 516, 147 in descending order are
mcqs.why: Greatest to smallest: 516 > 235 > 147, so descending order is 516, 235, 147.

lessons.title: One Thousand — the First 4-Digit Number
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

999 + 1 = 1000.
One thousand is the first and the smallest 4-digit number.

1000 = 1 thousand, 0 hundreds, 0 tens, 0 ones.

What I have learnt in Unit 1

  • Read and write ordinal numbers.
  • Count in words and numerals.
  • Use place value.
  • Compare and order numbers.
  • Count in 10s and 100s.
  • Recognise one thousand.

Vocabulary: Ordinal Numbers, Compare, Ascending Order, Descending Order.

lessons.title: Subtraction with Borrowing (2-Digit Numbers)
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Subtract the ones first, then the tens. If the ones digit of the first number is smaller, borrow 1 ten: the ones grow by 10 and the tens fall by 1.

Clue words for subtraction: left, how many more, how many less, how many fewer, remaining, difference.

Worked example: 15 - 8 (opener)

Step 1: 15 pencils - 8 pencils.
Step 2: 15 - 8 = 7.
Answer: 7 fewer pencils.

Worked example: 24 - 8
Step 1: The ones: 4 is smaller than 8, so borrow 1 ten. The ones become 14.
Step 2: 14 - 8 = 6.
Step 3: Subtract the tens: 1 - 0 = 1.
Answer: 24 - 8 = 16

Check the borrowing: ones become 14 because 1 ten is borrowed; 14 - 8 = 6; the tens are now 1 - 0 = 1. So 24 - 8 = 16.

Worked example: 42 - 15
Step 1: The ones: 2 is smaller than 5, so borrow 1 ten. The ones become 12.
Step 2: 12 - 5 = 7.
Step 3: Subtract the tens: 3 - 1 = 2.
Answer: 42 - 15 = 27

Here the apples example: ones become 12 after borrowing; 12 - 5 = 7; tens 3 - 1 = 2. So 42 - 15 = 27 apples.

Ones: 2 is smaller than 5, so borrow 1 ten; the ones become 12. 12 - 5 = 7. Tens: 3 - 1 = 2. So 42 - 15 = 27.

lessons.title: Division as Equal Sharing and Successive Subtraction
lessons.notes_html:
The rules

  • Division means sharing things equally. The symbol for division is /.
  • Division is also successive subtraction: keep subtracting the size of one share until nothing is left; the number of times you subtracted is the answer.
  • Multiplication helps us check division: if 2 x 4 = 8, then 8 / 4 = 2.

Worked example: biscuits (opener)

Step 1: 12 biscuits are shared equally in 3 boxes.
Step 2: Write the division: 12 / 3.
Step 3: In the table of 3, 3 x 4 = 12, so 12 / 3 = 4.
Answer: 4 biscuits in each box.

Worked example: 6 balloons among 3 children (successive subtraction)

Step 1: Start with 6 balloons: 6 - 3 = 3.
Step 2: Subtract once more: 3 - 3 = 0.
Step 3: We subtracted 3 two times, so 6 / 3 = 2.
Answer: Each child gets 2 balloons.

Worked example: 10 apples between 2 children

Step 1: 10 - 2 = 8.
Step 2: 8 - 2 = 6.
Step 3: 6 - 2 = 4.
Step 4: 4 - 2 = 2.
Step 5: 2 - 2 = 0. We subtracted 2 five times.
Answer: 10 / 2 = 5, so each child gets 5 apples.

Worked example: 8 carrots among 4 rabbits

Step 1: 8 - 4 = 4.
Step 2: 4 - 4 = 0. We subtracted 4 two times.
Step 3: So 8 / 4 = 2. Check: 2 x 4 = 8.
Answer: Each rabbit gets 2 carrots.

  • 20 eggs among 4 children = 20 / 4 = 5 eggs each.
  • 12 balloons among 3 children = 12 / 3 = 4 balloons each.

lessons.title: Clue Words for Number Stories — Choosing the Operation
lessons.notes_html:
Clue words — how to choose the operation

  • Addition clues: Total, Altogether, In all, Sum, Added to.
  • Subtraction clues: Left, More than, How many less, How many fewer, Remain, Difference.
  • Multiplication clues: Product, Times, In all, Altogether.
  • Division clues: How many will each get, How many in each group, Shared, Divided, Equal, Equally.

Steps to solve a number story

  1. Read the story carefully.
  2. Underline the clue words.
  3. Draw a picture if needed.
  4. Write a number sentence.
  5. Solve it.

Story 1 — addition

A tailor stitched 65 suits in one week and 58 suits in the next week. How many suits did he stitch altogether? The clue altogether means addition.

Step 1: Write the sum: 65 + 58.
Step 2: Add the ones: 5 + 8 = 13. Write 3 and carry 1 ten.
Step 3: Add the tens: 6 + 5 + 1 (carried) = 12.
Answer: He stitched 123 suits altogether.

Story 2 — subtraction

Ahmed had Rs 500. He spent Rs 225. How much money is left with him? The clue left means subtraction.

Step 1: Write the sum: 500 - 225.
Step 2: The ones: 0 is smaller than 5. Borrow across zero: the hundreds 5 becomes 4, the tens become 10, then borrow 1 ten so the ones become 10; 10 - 5 = 5.
Step 3: Subtract the tens: 9 - 2 = 7.
Step 4: Subtract the hundreds: 4 - 2 = 2.
Answer: Rs 275 is left with Ahmed.

Story 3 — multiplication

Ahmed has 5 books in a bag. How many books are there in 6 bags? The groups are equal, so we multiply.

Step 1: Write the product: 5 x 6.
Step 2: 5 x 6 = 30.
Answer: There are 30 books in 6 bags.

Story 4 — division

27 bananas are shared equally among 3 monkeys. How many bananas does each monkey get? The clue equally means division.

Step 1: Write the division: 27 / 3.
Step 2: 3 x 9 = 27, so 27 / 3 = 9.
Answer: Each monkey gets 9 bananas.

What I have learnt about division

  • Divide by successive subtraction.
  • Share equally.
  • Use the division symbol /.
  • A number divided by itself is 1.
  • A number divided by 1 is the number itself.

Vocabulary: Divide, Successive subtraction, Equally sharing.

The rule

A fraction is a part of a whole. The parts of a fraction must be equal parts.

Key fact: Equal parts have the same shape and the same size.

Worked example: two cakes

Hina divides a cake into two equal parts. Raza divides a cake into two unequal parts. Who divided the cake in equal parts? Hina — her two parts are the same size, so they can be named as fractions.

In the book's opener, Amna divides her birthday cake into three equal parts and gives them to her friends — each part is a fraction of the whole cake.

Shapes in unequal parts (from the book)

A triangle cut into uneven horizontal strips, a rectangle with uneven divisions, an oval with uneven divisions, a circle with uneven divisions, and a trapezium with uneven divisions — none of these parts can be named as equal fractions.

Shapes in equal parts (from the book)

A square divided into 4 equal squares, a circle divided into 2 equal halves, a hexagon divided into equal parts, a triangle divided into 2 equal parts, and a rectangle divided into 3 equal strips.

The rule

A fraction is written as: number of parts we take / total number of equal parts. The number above the line is the parts taken; the number below the line is the total equal parts.

Worked examples

  • A triangle has two equal parts; one part coloured = one-half = 1/2.
  • A circle has three equal parts; one part coloured = one-third = 1/3.
  • A square has four equal parts; one part coloured = one-quarter = 1/4.

  • Circle (4 parts) = 1/4
  • Heart (2 parts) = 1/2

lessons.title: Length — Metre and Centimetre
lessons.notes_html:
Why we need standard units

The car is longer than the motorbike, but to measure the exact length of objects we need standard units of length. Heights, too, are measured with an instrument — a measuring tape or a metre rod.

Metre

Rule: The metre is the standard unit of length. The symbol m is used for metre.

The lengths of rope, wire, ribbon and tables are measured in metres.

Key fact: The length, width and height of longer objects are measured in metres.

Centimetre

Rule: The symbol cm is used for centimetre. A school ruler is divided into 15 equal parts; the length of each part is 1 cm.

The lengths of a pencil, notebook and chocolate are measured in centimetres. In the book, the length of the chocolate is 8 cm.

Key facts: Centimetres are used to measure the lengths of shorter objects. 1 m = 100 cm.

Class activity: measure and record the lengths of classroom objects using a metre rod and a ruler, and find the longest and the shortest object (a student activity — there is no fixed answer).

The rule

Lengths can be added and subtracted like ordinary numbers, but both lengths must be in the same unit, and the answer keeps that unit.

lessons.title: Mass — Kilogram and Gram
lessons.notes_html:
Why we need a standard unit

To measure the accurate mass of objects, we need the standard unit of mass.

Kilogram

Rule: The standard unit of mass is the kilogram. The symbol kg is used for kilogram. It measures the mass of heavy objects like a flour bag and a watermelon.

Worked example: the mass of a watermelon is 6 kg and the mass of a bag of flour is 10 kg.
Step 1: To find how much more the flour is: 10 kg - 6 kg.
Step 2: 10 - 6 = 4.
Answer: The flour bag is 4 kg more than the watermelon.

Gram

Rule: The symbol g is used for gram. Gram measures the mass of lighter objects like a pencil and a biscuit. In the book, the mass of a biscuit pack is 300 g.

Key facts: Kilogram is used for heavy objects; gram is used for lighter objects. 1 kg = 1000 g.

Class activity: measure and record the mass of school bags and find the heaviest and the lightest (a student activity).

lessons.notes_html:
What is capacity?

Capacity is how much a container can hold. One jug fills three glasses of water, so the jug holds more water than a glass. A bucket holds more water than a bowl.

Key fact: The larger the container, the more capacity it will have.

Try Yourself — the container with more capacity: the bottle (against a glass), the kettle (against a cup), the big juice carton (against a small milk carton), the tub (against a small pot).

Litre

Rule: The litre is the standard unit of capacity. The symbol l is used for litre. Water, milk and petrol are measured in litres.

Millilitre

Rule: The symbol ml is used for millilitre. It measures the capacity of small containers; the capacity of a glass or a cup is measured in millilitres.

Key facts: The capacity of large containers is measured in litres and the capacity of small containers in millilitres. 1 litre = 1000 millilitres.

lessons.title: Hours and Minutes — Reading the Clock
lessons.notes_html:
The clock

The dial of the clock is divided into 12 big parts (the numbers 1 to 12). Each big part is further divided into 5 equal small parts, and one small part represents one minute. So the whole dial has 12 x 5 = 60 small parts.

The minute hand moves from one number to the next number in 5 minutes. When the minute hand completes one full round (60 minutes), the hour hand moves to the next number.

Key facts: 60 minutes = 1 hour. 24 hours = 1 day. There are 24 hours in a day because the hour hand completes two rounds in a day.

Worked example: Ahmad's breakfast clock

Step 1: The hour hand is at 8, so the hour is 8.
Step 2: The minute hand is at 3. Each number means 5 minutes, so 3 x 5 = 15 minutes.
Answer: The time is 8:15.

Morning and evening

Amna goes to school at 7 o'clock in the morning and does her homework at 5 o'clock in the evening. Morning time is written with a.m. and evening (afternoon/night) time with p.m. — this is explained fully in the a.m. and p.m. lesson.

There are 365 or 366 days in a solar year and 12 months in the year. A calendar is the record of all the months, dates and days of the year. To find the day of a date, find the month, then the date, then read the day written above it.

lessons.title: The Lunar (Hijri) Calendar
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

The lunar calendar is also known as the Hijri and Islamic calendar. There are 12 months in the lunar year and 29 or 30 days in a lunar month, depending on the sighting of the new moon.

Book correction: the book prints 'There are 354 or 365 days in a lunar year.' A lunar year is actually 354 or 355 days — the '365' here appears to be a misprint for 355.

The lunar months in order

  1. Muharram
  2. Safar
  3. Rabi-ul-Awwal
  4. Rabi-ul-Sani
  5. Jammadi-ul-Awwal
  6. Jammadi-ul-Sani
  7. Rajab
  8. Sha'ban
  9. Ramadan
  10. Shawwal
  11. Zul-Qadah
  12. Zul-Hajjah

Try Yourself — the day for each date (answers from the printed calendar)

  • 10 Muharram = Monday (given)
  • 18 Jammadi-ul-Awwal = Monday
  • 5 Safar = Thursday
  • 20 Jammadi-ul-Sani = Friday
  • 29 Rajab = Monday
  • 25 Rabi-ul-Sani = Sunday
  • 27 Ramadan = Tuesday
  • 12 Rabi-ul-Awwal = Saturday
  • 1 Shawwal = Friday
  • 19 Zul-Qadah = Thursday
  • 10 Zul-Hajjah = Wednesday
  • 25 Sha'ban = Saturday

Also: encircle the months in which we celebrate the Eids — Shawwal (Eid-ul-Fitr) and Zul-Hajjah (Eid-ul-Azha) — and tick Ramadan, the month in which Muslims fast.

What I have learnt in Unit 5 (Time)

  • Recognise hours in a day and minutes in an hour.
  • Read and write the time from a clock in hours and minutes (five-minute intervals).
  • Recognise a.m. and p.m.
  • Draw clock hands to show a given time.
  • Use the solar calendar and the Islamic calendar to find a particular date and day.

Vocabulary: a.m., p.m., Solar year, Lunar year, Calendar.

lessons.title: Shapes in the Picture — Counting Squares, Triangles, Circles and Rectangles
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

Look at a picture carefully and count each kind of shape wherever it appears — in the big objects and in the small parts as well. The four shapes in this unit are the square, the triangle, the circle and the rectangle.

Worked example: counting the shapes in the book's picture

  • Squares: 4 — 2 house windows + 2 in the bottom row.
  • Circles: 5 — the round tree top + the sun + 2 car wheels + 1 in the bottom row.
  • Rectangles: 10 — 4 tree trunks + the car body + the car cabin middle + the house body + the house door + 2 in the bottom row.
  • Triangles: 13 — left tree 2 + middle tree 1 + right tree 1 + car cabin sides 2 + house roof 1 + bottom row 6.

Note: the lower part of the left tree is drawn with a flat top (a cut-off triangle). It is counted here as a triangle to fit the book's four-shape table; counted strictly, the triangles would be 12.

mcqs.why: Count the squares: 2 + 2 = 4 (2 house windows and 2 in the bottom row).

mcqs.why: Count the rectangles: 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 10 (4 tree trunks, the car body, the car cabin middle, the house body, the house door, 2 in the bottom row).

mcqs.why: Count the triangles: 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 6 = 13 (left tree 2, middle tree 1, right tree 1, car cabin sides 2, house roof 1, bottom row 6).

lessons.title: Semi-Circle and Quarter-Circle
lessons.notes_html:
The rules

Divide a circle into two equal parts; one half part of the circle is called a semi-circle.

Divide a circle into four equal parts; one quarter part of the circle is called a quarter-circle.

Try Yourself — count and colour (answers)

Colour the circle red, the semi-circle green and the quarter-circle yellow. The totals in the book's picture are:

  • Circles: 8 — locomotive wheels 3 + middle figure 1 + crab eyes 2 + crab feet 2.
  • Semi-circles: 4 — glass bowl + glass base + locomotive dome + crab body.
  • Quarter-circles: 9 — locomotive front 1 + middle figure 4 + bottom dome halves 2 + crab claws 2.

Note: the locomotive's blue body also has two white semi-circular cut-outs; if those are counted as semi-circles too, the semi-circles would be 6 instead of 4.

lessons.title: Sides and Vertices of Shapes + Exercise 1
lessons.notes_html:
The rules

  • The corner of any shape is called a vertex. The plural of side is sides and the plural of vertex is vertices.
  • Rectangle: 4 sides and 4 vertices. Its opposite sides are equal in length.
  • Square: 4 sides and 4 vertices. All its sides are equal in length.
  • Triangle: 3 sides and 3 vertices. Its sides may or may not be equal in length.
  • Circle: 0 sides and 0 vertices — it has one curved boundary and no corners.

Exercise 1 — 2-D shapes (answers in the shapes' own words)

  • Square: 'My name is square. I have 4 sides and 4 vertices. All my sides are equal in length.'
  • Triangle: 'I have 3 sides and 3 vertices. Who am I? Triangle.'
  • Rectangle: 'I am a rectangle. I have 4 sides and 4 vertices.'
  • Oval (Try Yourself): 'My name is oval. I have 0 sides and 0 vertices.'

lessons.title: Straight and Curved Lines + Exercise 2
lessons.notes_html:
The rules

A thread pulled tightly in both hands is like a straight line. A thread held loose is like a curved line.

Straight lines can be horizontal, vertical or slanting. Curved lines bend in many ways.

Exercise 2 — matching (answers)

Straight lines: the slanting, vertical and horizontal straight lines. Curved lines: the wavy line, the S-shaped line and the arc lines.

Count the straight and curved lines (answers)

  • (a) Curved diamond shape: straight lines 2, curved lines 2.
  • (b) Vase: straight lines 2 (the top rim and the base), curved lines 2 (the two sides).
  • (c) Dome with two small side domes: straight lines 1 (the base line), curved lines 3 (the big dome arc + 2 small arcs).

Count again (answers)

  • (a) Square: straight lines 4, curved lines 0.
  • (b) Semi-circle: straight lines 1 (the base), curved lines 1 (the arc).
  • (c) Triangle: straight lines 3, curved lines 0.

Drawing a straight line: use a ruler. We measure and draw a straight line with the help of the ruler.

lessons.title: Measuring and Drawing Straight Lines + Exercise 3
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

To measure and draw a straight line with a ruler, we always start from 0 cm.

Worked example: measuring a line

Step 1: Place the ruler along the line with 0 at its start.
Step 2: The line ends at the 6 mark.
Answer: The length of the line is 6 cm.

Worked example: drawing an 8 cm line

Step 1: Hold the ruler firmly on the paper.
Step 2: Put the pencil at 0 cm.
Step 3: Draw a straight line along the ruler up to 8 cm.
Step 4: Remove the ruler.

(a) 5 cm. (b) 7 cm. (c) 12 cm. These lengths are as printed in the book at full size, so they depend on the print size.

Exercise 3 — draw with a ruler

Draw: (a) a 4 cm straight line; (b) a 6 cm straight line; (c) a 10 cm straight line. Method: place the ruler's 0 at the start point and draw to the required mark.

lessons.title: Patterns + Exercise 4
lessons.notes_html:
The rule

A pattern is a set of shapes that repeats in a fixed order. To complete a pattern, first find the part that repeats, then write or draw the same part again. A pattern can change in shape, in size, in direction (orientation), in colour, or in more than one of these together.

The book's patterns

  • Change in shape: big yellow triangle, small yellow square, repeating.
  • Change in size: big blue quarter-circle, small blue quarter-circle, repeating.
  • Change in direction: green triangle pointing right, green triangle pointing up, repeating.
  • Change in shape and colour: red semi-circle, brown rectangle, repeating.
  • Change in size and colour: small orange rectangle (2 squares), big purple rectangle (6 squares), repeating.

Exercise 4 — complete the grid patterns (answers: what comes next in each row)

  • Row 1 (blue): a horizontal bar of 3 squares, then a vertical bar of 2 squares, repeating — next: a horizontal 3-square bar, then a vertical 2-square bar.
  • Row 2 (red): a red triangle (2 squares wide), a red square, repeating — next: a red triangle, then a red square.
  • Row 3 (purple): a horizontal bar of 2 squares, then a vertical bar of 2 squares, repeating — next: a horizontal 2-square bar, then a vertical 2-square bar.
  • Row 4 (green/yellow): a green 2x2 block, a yellow right-triangle (2x2), repeating — next: a green 2x2 block, then a yellow triangle.
  • Row 5 (red/blue): a red triangle (2x2), a blue 2x2 block, repeating — next: a red triangle, then a blue block.
  • Row 6 (brown/green): a brown right-triangle, a green right-triangle, repeating — next: a brown triangle, then a green triangle.
  • Row 7 (yellow/red): a yellow trapezoid, a red triangle, repeating — next: a yellow trapezoid, then a red triangle.
